english: I think / it seems / it looks like (a softened guess or opinion)
formNote: Literally 'it is like the thing that...' (것 = thing/fact, 같다 = to be like/same), so you are framing your statement as a resemblance to truth rather than a flat fact — that hedge is the whole point and is why Koreans reach for it constantly. The form tracks tense on the modifier: present verb takes -는 (가는 것 같아요), adjective and past verb take -(으)ㄴ (추운 것 같아요, 먹은 것 같아요), and a future/probability guess takes -(으)ㄹ (올 것 같아요). Contrast it with the blunter guess word 같다 used as -겠- (오겠어요 'it'll surely come') and with -나 보다/-(으)ㄴ가 보다, which infer from outside evidence ('looks like, judging by what I see'); -는 것 같다 is your own soft impression, even about your own feelings (저 그 사람 좋아하는 것 같아요 = I think I like him). Register: neutral-polite and very safe, so people even soften their own opinions with it to avoid sounding pushy. The English-speaker trap is treating it as 'I think THAT (a clause)' and trying to keep a full sentence + 라고 생각해요; here the clause must be squeezed into a modifier before 것. In speech 것 almost always shrinks to 거: -는 거 같아요.
usage: Adjective 맛있다 + present-style -는 (a fixed exception); softer than a flat 맛있어요
Plain adjective takes -ㄴ 것 같아요, never -는
A guess about the future → -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요
examples: 이거 좀 매운 것 같아요.
I think this is a little spicy.
Simplest shape: adjective + -ㄴ 것 같아요 to soften a plain judgement
저 둘 사귀는 거 같지 않아?
Don't those two seem to be dating?
Casual 거 + present -는, tagged with -지 않아? to fish for agreement
제가 길을 잘못 든 것 같은데, 여기 어디예요?
I think I took a wrong turn — where is this?
Real situation: hedging your own mistake with 같은데 before asking for help
mistakes: Using -는 것 같다 with a plain adjective: 춥는 것 같아요 is wrong — descriptive adjectives take -(으)ㄴ, so it is 추운 것 같아요. (맛있다/재미있다 are the exception that keep -는 because they end in 있다.)
Building it like English 'I think that...': saying 비가 온다고 것 같아요 by stuffing a finished clause in front. The clause has to become a single modifier: 비가 오는 것 같아요.
Mismatching tense on the modifier: for something already done, 가는 것 같아요 ('seems to be going') is wrong if they already left — use the past 간 것 같아요.

english: decided to / made up my mind to (often a plan or promise)
formNote: Here -기 turns the verb into a noun ('the doing of X') and -로 marks it as the direction/terms you settled on, so the literal feel is 'I set things toward doing X' — a resolution or an arrangement. Attach -기로 하다 straight onto any verb stem with zero sound change (운동하다 → 운동하기로, 끊다 → 끊기로), then report it in the past, 했어요, because the deciding is already done; the present 하다 (-기로 해요) reads as 'let's decide to / it's agreed that we'll', a softer proposal, which is the key contrast learners miss. Compare -(으)ㄹ게요 'I'll (promise to you, here and now)' and -(으)려고 해요 'I intend/plan to': -기로 했어요 is the firmest — a concluded decision or a mutual pact, often a New Year's resolution or a plan made with others (같이 가기로 했어요). It also commonly pairs with 약속하다 and 마음먹다. Negative puts the negation INSIDE the embedded clause — 안 V-기로 했어요 (안 가기로 했어요) or the smoother V-지 않기로 했어요 (가지 않기로 했어요); don't move 안 outside as V-기로 안 했어요, which flips the meaning to 'didn't decide to V'. English-speaker pitfall: don't translate 'decided' with 결정했어요 every time — 결정하다 is heavy/formal (a board decides a policy); everyday personal resolutions overwhelmingly use -기로 했어요.
usage: I decided to cut down on drinking
A very common New Year goal; 줄이다 = reduce
Mutual agreement — the 'pact' use between people
I decided not to work overtime
Negative via 안; the smoother form is 야근하지 않기로 했어요
examples: 저 다음 달부터 운동하기로 했어요.
I've decided to start working out next month.
Simple resolution: bare stem + -기로 했어요
우리 다음 주에 한강 가서 치맥 하기로 했어.
We decided to do chicken and beer at the Han River next week.
Group plan; 치맥 = fried chicken + beer, a staple young-adult outing
회사랑 얘기해서 재택근무하기로 했어요.
I talked with the company and we settled on me working from home.
Real arrangement reached with someone else; 재택근무 = WFH
mistakes: Saying -기로 해요 (present) for a decision you already made — that sounds like a fresh proposal ('let's decide to'). A settled decision needs the past -기로 했어요.
Inserting a vowel like -으로: it is always -기로, attached directly to the stem (먹기로 했어요), never 먹으기로.
Reaching for 결정했어요 for casual everyday choices ('I decided to nap'). 결정하다 sounds like a formal/official ruling; for personal resolve use 낮잠 자기로 했어요.

english: ended up (completely) doing it — finished it off, often with regret or relief
formNote: 버리다 on its own means 'to throw away', and as an auxiliary it keeps that flavor: the action is done all the way, finished off, gone past the point of return — and that completeness carries emotion, either regret ('darn, I went and did it') or relief ('there, it's finally off my plate'). Build it by taking the verb's -아/어 connector and adding 버리다: stems with ㅏ/ㅗ take -아 버리다 (가다 → 가 버리다, 오다 → 와 버리다), other stems take -어 버리다 (먹다 → 먹어 버리다, 잊다 → 잊어 버리다), and 하다 → 해 버리다. Contrast its sibling -아/어 두다/놓다, which means doing something and leaving it ready ('do it in advance and keep it'), the opposite mood from 버리다's 'do it and be rid of it'; and note that 버리다 colors the feeling, while -았/었어요 alone just reports the fact. It loves 다, 그냥, 벌써 (다 먹어 버렸어요, 그냥 가 버렸어요). English-speaker pitfall: there is no English auxiliary for this, so learners drop it — but plain 다 썼어요 'I spent it all' loses the rueful punch of 다 써 버렸어요 'I went and blew it all'. Spacing matters too: write 버리다 as a separate word from the -아/어 form.
usage: I ended up eating it all
Guilty confession; 다 + 버리다 = polished off, oops
Sudden, decisive, gone — 그냥 underlines the abruptness
까먹다 = forget; 버리다 stresses it's irretrievably gone
I just got it all done
The relief use — finished it off and it's off my hands
examples: 접시를 깨 버렸어요.
I went and broke the plate.
Simple regret: a clean -어 버렸어요 confession of an accident
월급 들어오자마자 다 써 버렸어요.
I blew my whole paycheck the moment it came in.
Everyday money regret; -자마자 'as soon as' + 다 써 버리다
고백했는데 차여 버렸어... 술이나 마시자.
I confessed but got rejected... let's just drink.
Real emotional scene; 차이다 = get dumped, 버리다 lands the gut-punch
mistakes: Mangling the vowel join: it's 가 버렸어요 (not 가어 버렸어요) and 와 버렸어요 (not 오아 버렸어요) — apply the normal ㅏ/ㅗ → -아 contraction first.
Writing it as one word, 가버렸어요 / 먹어버렸어요. Standard spelling keeps the auxiliary separate: 가 버렸어요.
Dropping 버리다 because English has no equivalent, so 다 썼어요 comes out flat. If you mean the regretful 'I went and spent it all', you need 다 써 버렸어요.

english: I'm worried that... / in case... (anxiety about something happening)
formNote: This is the wondering ending -(으)ㄹ까 ('I wonder if...') frozen in front of 보다 ('to see/consider'), so the literal nuance is 'considering that maybe X might happen' — and what falls out is anxiety: you are bracing for an unwanted possibility. Attach -ㄹ까 봐(요) to vowel-ending stems (가다 → 갈까 봐, 오다 → 올까 봐) and -을까 봐(요) to consonant stems (늦다 → 늦을까 봐, 밀리다 → 밀릴까 봐); for a worry about something already over use -았/었을까 봐요 (놓쳤을까 봐요 = worried I missed it). The sharp contrast to memorize is with the look-alike question -(으)ㄹ까요? 'shall we? / I wonder, do you think?' (갈까요? = shall we go?) — same syllables, totally different job: -ㄹ까 봐요 is never a question, it states a fear. Mid-sentence it becomes -(으)ㄹ까 봐(서) + the precaution you take because of the fear (비 올까 봐 우산 챙겼어요). It also pairs naturally with 걱정하다/불안하다. English-speaker pitfall: don't render 'in case' with 만약 + a conditional; 'in case it rains' is 비 올까 봐, and crucially the worry clause must describe a bad/unwanted outcome — you wouldn't use it for something you hope for.
usage: I brought an umbrella in case it rains
I don't eat it because I'm afraid of gaining weight
I didn't say it for fear of getting scolded
혼나다 = get scolded; fear drives the silence
examples: 감기 걸릴까 봐 옷 따뜻하게 입었어요.
I dressed warmly in case I catch a cold.
Simple worry + precaution; clean -(으)ㄹ까 봐 chain
답장 안 오길래 차단당했을까 봐 걱정했잖아.
You didn't reply, so I was worried I'd been blocked.
Past worry → -았을까 봐; 차단당하다 = get blocked on a messenger
월세 밀릴까 봐 알바 하나 더 구했어요.
I picked up another part-time job in case I fall behind on rent.
Real-life money anxiety; 월세 = monthly rent, 알바 = part-time gig
mistakes: Confusing it with the suggestion/question -(으)ㄹ까요?. 갈까요? = 'shall we go?'; 갈까 봐요 = 'I'm worried (someone/I) might go'. Same sound, opposite function — one asks, one frets.
Using it for a good outcome you want, e.g. 합격할까 봐 기뻐요 to mean 'I'm happy I might pass'. The clause must be an unwanted possibility; for a hope, restructure (합격하면 좋겠어요).
Forgetting the past layer when the worry is about something already finished: 시험 망칠까 봐 ('worried I'll bomb the exam, future') vs 시험 망쳤을까 봐 ('worried I bombed it, already taken').

english: (someone) said that... — reporting a statement someone made
formNote: This is indirect (reported) speech: -다고 quotes the content of a plain-style statement and 하다 ('to say') frames it, so you relay what someone declared without their exact words or politeness level. The endings split by word class, which is the heart of the pattern: present-tense VERBS take -ㄴ다고/-는다고 (가다 → 간다고 했어요, 먹다 → 먹는다고 했어요), but ADJECTIVES and 이다 attach plain -다고 (춥다 → 춥다고 했어요), and the past is -았/었다고 했어요 for both. Nouns use N(이)라고 했어요. The contrast that trips learners is the question version -냐고 했어요 ('asked whether...') — statements report with -다고, questions with -냐고, and mixing them is the classic reported-speech error. In casual speech everything contracts to -대(요): 간대요 (= 간다고 해요), 바쁘대 (= 바쁘다고 해), a form you'll hear far more than the full one. English-speaker pitfall: English lets you say 'He said he's busy' with a full clause and backshift the tense; Korean does NOT backshift and instead demands you re-plain-style the inner verb (그가 바쁘다고 했어요), and beginners forget that present verbs cannot stay bare -다고 — it must be -ㄴ다고/-는다고.
usage: Noun → N(이)라고; 이래요 is the contraction of 이라고 해요
examples: 엄마가 오늘 일찍 온다고 했어요.
Mom said she's coming home early today.
Simple present-verb report → -ㄴ다고 했어요
팀장님이 오늘 회식 있다고 했어요.
The team lead said there's a company dinner today.
있다 patterns as -다고; 회식 = team dinner, core work word
걔가 너 좋아한다고 했어! 진짜야.
He said he likes you! For real.
Casual gossip; 좋아하다 → 좋아한다고, 걔 = that person/he
mistakes: Leaving a present-tense verb bare: 가다고 했어요 is wrong — present verbs need -ㄴ다고/-는다고, so 간다고 했어요 / 먹는다고 했어요.
Backshifting like English ('he said he WAS busy' → past). Korean keeps the original tense the speaker used: if he said '바빠요', you report 바쁘다고 했어요, not 바빴다고.
Using -다고 to report a question. 'He asked if I'd eaten' is 먹었냐고 했어요, never 먹었다고 했어요 (which means 'he SAID he'd eaten').

english: (someone) asked whether/if... — reporting a question someone asked
formNote: This is the question half of reported speech: -냐고 quotes someone's question and 하다 (or, more pointedly, 묻다/물어보다 'to ask') frames it. Modern colloquial Korean has flattened the endings, so you attach -냐고 to verb and adjective stems alike (가다 → 가냐고 했어요, 바쁘다 → 바쁘냐고 했어요); the older textbook split kept -느냐고 for verbs and -(으)냐고 for adjectives, which you'll still see in writing and in the formal 했습니다 column, but in speech -냐고 covers everything. Past is -았/었냐고 했어요, and nouns take N(이)냐고 했어요. The crucial contrast is with -다고 했어요, the STATEMENT version: a reported question must end -냐고 (오냐고 했어요 'asked if I'm coming') and a reported statement -다고 (온다고 했어요 'said he's coming') — this is the single most-confused boundary in indirect speech. Casually it contracts to -냬(요): 가냬 (= 가냐고 해), 남친 있냬 (= 있냐고 해). English-speaker pitfall: English buries the question with 'whether/if' and reorders it to statement word order ('asked WHETHER I had eaten'); Korean instead keeps the plain question intact and just clips on -냐고, and it does not switch to -다고 just because the sentence now looks declarative.
usage: Reporting a question that contains a question word (언제)
물어보다 fits the 'asked' frame more naturally than 하다
He's asking if I have a boyfriend
Casual -냬요, the everyday contraction of -냐고 해요
She asked why I didn't come
examples: 친구가 지금 뭐 하냐고 했어요.
My friend asked what I'm doing right now.
Simple wh-question report; 하다 → 하냐고
소개팅남이 무슨 일 하냐고 했어요.
The blind-date guy asked what I do for work.
Everyday social scene; 소개팅 = set-up date, 무슨 일 해요? relayed
엄마가 자꾸 취업 언제 하냐고 물어봐서 스트레스야.
My mom keeps asking when I'll get a job — it's stressful.
Real recurring pressure; 자꾸 = keeps on, 취업 = getting hired
mistakes: Reporting a question with -다고 instead of -냐고. 'She asked if I came' is 왔냐고 했어요; 왔다고 했어요 means 'she SAID I came' — a completely different message.
Over-applying the old -느냐고 in casual speech: 가느냐고 했어 sounds stiff/literary. Everyday spoken Korean just says 가냐고 했어.
Forgetting that wh-words stay inside the quote in their normal spot: it's 언제 오냐고 했어요, not a reordered '...whether when...' calque from English.

english: it's worth doing / good enough to / can be done (reasonably)
formNote: 만하다 here means 'to be worth / be of a level that justifies it', so V-(으)ㄹ 만하다 says the action is worth the effort, or at least decent and tolerable — note that 'decent' often means faint praise, not glowing. Attach -ㄹ 만하다 to vowel-ending stems (보다 → 볼 만하다, 가다 → 갈 만하다) and -을 만하다 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹을 만하다, 참다 → 참을 만하다); the past is -(으)ㄹ 만했어요. Two contrasts sharpen it: don't confuse this 만하다 (one word, 'worth doing', after -(으)ㄹ) with the size-comparison 만하다 ('as big as', as in 손바닥만 하다); and weigh it against the stronger -(으)ㄹ 가치가 있다 'has real value/merit' — -(으)ㄹ 만하다 is lighter, the register of 'eh, it's worth a look' or 'edible enough'. It leans on the future-potential modifier -(으)ㄹ precisely because you're judging whether doing it would pay off. English-speaker pitfall: learners grab the present modifier -는 (보는 만해요) by analogy with 'worth watching', but the slot needs -(으)ㄹ (볼 만해요); also beware reading 먹을 만해요 as enthusiastic — to a Korean it's lukewarm, 'it'll do'.
usage: Endorsing a place as worth the trip
A tolerable level of discomfort; 참다 = endure
examples: 이 영화 한 번쯤 볼 만해요.
This movie's worth a watch at least once.
Simple recommendation; vowel stem 보다 → 볼 만해요
회사 멀긴 한데 그래도 다닐 만해요.
The company's far, but it's still manageable to commute to.
Everyday realism; 다니다 = commute/attend, -긴 한데 concedes a downside
여기 가성비 좋아서 자주 올 만해요.
The value here is great, so it's worth coming back often.
Real endorsement; 가성비 = bang-for-buck, a huge young-adult buzzword
mistakes: Using the present modifier -는: 보는 만해요 / 먹는 만해요 is wrong. The slot takes the future-potential -(으)ㄹ → 볼 만해요, 먹을 만해요.
Reading 먹을 만해요 as strong praise. It's deliberately mild ('it'll do, it's passable'); for real praise say 맛있어요 or 진짜 맛있어요.
Confusing it with the size 만하다: 너만 하다 ('about as big as you') is a different word — the 'worth doing' one always follows -(으)ㄹ and is written 만하다 as one unit.

english: (it) ended up / came to be that... — a change of state, often not fully by your own choice
formNote: 되다 means 'to become / come about', so V-게 되다 frames an outcome as something that turned out that way through circumstances, not pure personal will — which is exactly why it sounds humble and is the polite default for explaining how your life changed. Attach -게 되다 to any verb stem (알다 → 알게 되다, 살다 → 살게 되다) and report the result in the past, -게 됐어요 (a contraction of -게 되었어요); present/future are -게 돼요 / -게 될 거예요. The contrast to nail is against a bare past verb and against -기로 했어요: 살았어요 just states 'I lived', 살기로 했어요 says 'I (actively) decided to live (there)', while 살게 됐어요 says 'it came about that I live there' — same event, but 게 됐어요 quietly removes the spotlight from your own decision, which Koreans prefer when announcing things (회사를 그만두게 됐어요 softens 'I quit'). It often appears with 우연히, 결국, 어쩌다 보니. English-speaker pitfall: learners translate it as plain 'became' and drop 되다, collapsing 알게 됐어요 'I came to know' into 알았어요 'I knew/found out' — and they overuse the willful 결정했어요 where a modest 게 됐어요 is the socially smoother choice.
usage: I ended up living in Korea
A life change framed modestly, not as your own doing
I came to find out that fact
Discovery that unfolded over time; 알게 되다 ≠ 알다
I ended up quitting the company
Softens a big personal decision into 'circumstances led to it'
Gradual, unforced change; pairs with 자연스럽게
examples: 요즘 운동을 자주 하게 됐어요.
These days I've come to exercise often.
Simple gradual change; bare stem + -게 됐어요
일 때문에 서울에서 살게 됐어요.
Because of work, I ended up living in Seoul.
Everyday self-intro for a newcomer; 때문에 supplies the circumstance
우연히 같은 동호회 하다가 사귀게 됐어요.
We happened to be in the same club and ended up dating.
Real story; 우연히 = by chance, 동호회 = hobby club, -다가 'in the middle of'
mistakes: Dropping 되다 and using the plain past: 알았어요 means 'I knew / found out (at a point)', whereas 알게 됐어요 means 'I gradually came to know' — the 되다 carries the 'came about' meaning.
Confusing it with the active decision -기로 했어요. 그만두기로 했어요 = 'I decided to quit (my choice)'; 그만두게 됐어요 = 'it ended up that I quit (circumstances)'. Pick by how much agency you want to claim.
Forcing 결정했어요 / 됐어요 mixes: you don't need both. For 'I ended up doing X' just say X-게 됐어요; adding 결정 reintroduces the willfulness the pattern is designed to soften.

english: while you're at it / since you're already doing it anyway
formNote: 김 here is the noun 'occasion/opportunity created by an action', so -(으)ㄴ 김에 means 'taking advantage of the fact that you've (already) done X, also do Y' — the second clause is the real point, riding for free on the first. Attach -ㄴ 김에 to vowel-ending stems (나오다 → 나온 김에) and -은 김에 to consonant stems (씻다 → 씻은 김에); a present, ongoing action takes -는 김에 (청소하는 김에 'while I'm cleaning anyway'). The set phrase 말 나온 김에 ('since it's come up in conversation') is worth memorizing whole. Contrast it with two near-misses: -(으)면서 means doing two things simultaneously and equally ('while/as'), whereas 김에 is opportunistic and tilts toward the add-on; and -(으)니까 just gives a reason ('since/because'), without the 'might as well piggyback' flavor. English-speaker pitfall: the literal logic 'since you WILL go anyway' tempts learners to use the future -(으)ㄹ 김에, but 김에 attaches to the completed/initiated action with -(으)ㄴ (or ongoing -는) — say 가는 김에 / 나온 김에, never 갈 김에. It also pairs naturally with 이왕 ('seeing as you're at it') for extra emphasis.
usage: Set phrase to tack on an errand
since you came, let's at least eat
온 김에 + a casual suggestion; -이나 = '(at least) something like'
Very common discourse opener for raising a related topic
Present -는 김에 for an action still in progress
examples: 일어난 김에 물 좀 마셨어요.
Since I was up anyway, I had some water.
Simplest shape: -(으)ㄴ 김에 + the free add-on action
편의점 가는 김에 내 커피도 하나 사다 줘.
Since you're heading to the store, grab me a coffee too.
Everyday favor; 가는 김에 (ongoing) + 사다 주다 'buy and bring'
말 나온 김에 우리 회식 날짜 정해요.
Since it's come up, let's set the date for the team dinner.
Real meeting-room move; the fixed 말 나온 김에 to seize the moment
mistakes: Using the future -(으)ㄹ 김에 for a plan: 갈 김에 is wrong. 김에 rides on a started/finished action, so use -(으)ㄴ (나온 김에) or ongoing -는 (가는 김에).

Swapping it for -(으)면서: 나오면서 커피 샀어요 means you bought coffee in the very act of going out (simultaneous). 나온 김에 커피 샀어요 means 'seeing as I was already out, I (also) bought coffee' — the opportunistic add-on the pattern is for.
Putting the main message in the first clause. The point lives in the SECOND clause; 밥 먹은 김에 산책했어요 highlights the walk, not the meal — don't structure it backwards.

english: to the extent/point that... / so much that...
formNote: 정도 is the Sino-Korean noun 程度 (程 'degree' + 度 'measure'), literally 'degree/measure', so A/V-(으)ㄹ 정도로 sets a vivid 'enough-to' benchmark that conveys how intense something is — you describe a degree by naming what it could reach. Attach -ㄹ 정도로 to vowel-ending stems (아프다 → 아플 정도로) and -을 정도로 to consonant stems (죽다 → 죽을 정도로); the benchmark clause comes first and the thing being measured follows (죽을 정도로 피곤해요 = tired to the point of dying). You can also close a sentence with -(으)ㄹ 정도예요 'it's to that extent'. Contrast it with -(으)ㄹ 만큼, which is very close ('as much as / to the degree that') but more neutral/quantitative and often interchangeable, whereas -(으)ㄹ 정도로 leans expressive and is the go-to for hyperbole (죽을 정도로, 미칠 정도로); and don't confuse 정도 here with 정도 meaning 'about/approximately' (한 시간 정도 'about an hour'). It rides the future-potential modifier -(으)ㄹ because the benchmark is a hypothetical reach, not a real event. English-speaker pitfall: learners drop in the present -는 (아프는 정도로) by habit, but the slot needs -(으)ㄹ (아플 정도로); and they try to map it onto 'so ... that' word order — in Korean the 'that' clause (the degree) goes FIRST, before the predicate it modifies.
usage: I'm dead tired (tired to the point of dying)
Stock hyperbole; benchmark 죽을 정도로 precedes 피곤해요
I laughed so hard I teared up
to the point of being speechless
I ate till I was about to burst
배 터지다 = stomach bursting; classic overeating line
examples: 오늘 손이 시릴 정도로 추워요.
It's cold enough today to make your hands sting.
Simple adjective benchmark; 시리다 = sting from cold, 추워요 follows
어제 클럽에서 목 쉴 정도로 소리 질렀어요.
Last night at the club I screamed so much my voice went hoarse.
Everyday nightlife; 목 쉬다 = lose one's voice, verb stem + -ㄹ 정도로
발표 전에 손이 떨릴 정도로 긴장했어요.
Before the presentation I was so nervous my hands were shaking.
Real work/uni scene; the 손이 떨릴 정도로 benchmark measures 긴장했어요
mistakes: Using the present modifier -는: 아프는 정도로 / 죽는 정도로 is wrong. The slot takes the future-potential -(으)ㄹ → 아플 정도로, 죽을 정도로.
Mixing it up with 정도 'about/approximately'. 한 시간 정도 = 'about an hour'; the degree pattern is -(으)ㄹ 정도로 attached to a verb/adjective stem — different 정도.
Ordering it like English 'so X that Y': putting the result first. In Korean the degree clause leads (눈물 날 정도로 웃었어요), then the predicate it intensifies — not 웃었어요 정도로 눈물 날.
